title: J. W. Hampton, Jr., & Co. v. United States (1928)
shortTitle: J. W. Hampton, Jr., & Co. v. United States (1928)
summary: The Court upheld tariff adjustments guided by Congress’s policy of equalizing production costs and articulated the intelligible-principle formulation.
notes: Chief Justice Taft wrote for a unanimous Court; the rule statement is verbatim: "If Congress shall lay down by legislative act an intelligible principle to which the person or body authorized to fix such rates is directed to conform, such legislative action is not a forbidden delegation of legislative power."

sections.Parties: J. W. Hampton, Jr., & Co., an importer of barium dioxide, challenged additional duties assessed by a federal customs collector under a presidential tariff proclamation.
sections.Material Facts: The 1922 Tariff Act authorized adjustments to equalize differences between domestic and foreign production costs, bounded changes at fifty percent of statutory rates, identified relevant cost factors, and required a Tariff Commission investigation with notice and an opportunity for interested parties to be heard. After the Commission investigated, President Coolidge found that the principal competing country was Germany and raised the duty on barium dioxide from four to six cents per pound. The importer contested the additional two cents.
sections.Procedural History: The Customs Court upheld the statute, and the Court of Customs Appeals affirmed. The Supreme Court granted certiorari and affirmed the judgment, sustaining the assessment against the delegation challenge.
sections.Issue: Could Congress authorize the President to adjust tariff rates within specified limits to implement a statutory policy of equalizing production costs?
sections.Holding: Yes. A delegation complies with the separation of powers when Congress supplies an intelligible principle directing the authorized actor’s exercise of authority. The policy and constraints here supplied that guidance.
sections.Reasoning: The Court considered changing production costs an implementation problem for which Congress could seek executive assistance. Congress specified the equalization policy, the relevant considerations, the investigative machinery, and a numerical limit. The Court saw no special nondelegation bar for tariff or taxing legislation. Its coordination analysis emphasized practical governmental necessities without abandoning the allocation of legislative power to Congress. The accompanying Jaffe note questions how determinate the supposedly clear standard really was: cost allocation, the meaning of equalization, presidential initiative, and the treatment of Commission findings left significant choices. The holding and that scholarly criticism should be kept distinct.

topics.lrs-s-intelligible-principle: The decision names the intelligible-principle test and applies it to a cost-equalization policy with procedural and numerical limits.
topics.lrs-s-conditional-legislation: Hampton treats the President's cost-equalization adjustments as executing a congressional policy, extending Field v. Clark's contingency reasoning.
topics.lrs-s-article-i-vesting: The intelligible-principle test is the Court's account of what Article I's vesting of legislative power forbids and permits.
